title: Interview with a Museum Curator
description: A museum announcement, a radio interview with a curator, a staff discussion about an exhibition and a talk about looking after objects.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Museum announcement
parts.intro: You will hear a recorded announcement at a city museum.

script.speaker: Voice
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to the City History Museum. Before you begin your visit, here is some useful information.

script.speaker: Voice
script.text: The museum has three floors. The ground floor houses our permanent collection, which tells the story of the city from its beginnings as a river port. On the first floor you will find our temporary exhibition, which changes every four months.

script.speaker: Voice
script.text: Please note that the second floor is closed this week for repairs to the roof. We apologise for the inconvenience, and visitors may use the lift to reach the café, which has moved to the ground floor.

script.speaker: Voice
script.text: Photography is welcome in most galleries, but please do not use a flash, as bright light can damage old paper and fabric. You may not take photographs in the textile room at all.

script.speaker: Voice
script.text: Guided tours leave from the main desk every day at eleven o'clock and again at two o'clock. They last about forty-five minutes, and they are free, although we do ask for a small donation if you enjoyed the tour.

script.speaker: Voice
script.text: Finally, today at three o'clock our curator will give a short talk about the new exhibition. Seats are limited, so please arrive early. Thank you, and enjoy your visit.

parts.title: Part 2 · Radio interview with a curator
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Linh, interviewing a museum curator, Dr James Cole.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Dr Cole, most of us picture a curator as someone in a quiet room, surrounded by old objects. Is that accurate?

script.speaker: James
script.text: Partly, I suppose. I do spend time with objects, but if I'm honest, I spend far more time answering emails, writing labels and persuading people to lend us things. It's much less romantic than it sounds.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: What exactly is a curator's job?

script.speaker: James
script.text: Essentially, we decide which stories the museum tells. We choose objects, research them, and arrange them so that visitors can understand something new. An object alone is just an object. It becomes interesting when you place it next to another one and the connection becomes clear.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: How did you get into the profession?

script.speaker: James
script.text: By accident, really. I studied history at university and I wanted to teach. But I volunteered at a small local museum during the summer holidays, and I was lucky enough to be given a box of letters from the First World War to catalogue. I was hooked.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Is there an object in the collection that you particularly love?

script.speaker: James
script.text: Yes, a very ordinary one. It's a child's wooden toy boat from the nineteenth century. It's scratched, with a bit of string still attached. It reminds me that history isn't only about kings and battles. It's also about people who played, and cooked, and worried about their children.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: What's the biggest challenge in your work?

script.speaker: James
script.text: Deciding what to leave out. We can display only about five per cent of the collection at any time. Every choice means that something wonderful stays in a box in the basement.

parts.title: Part 3 · Staff discussion about a new exhibition
parts.intro: You will hear two museum staff, Mai and Tom, discussing an exhibition about the local river.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Mai, have you seen the draft plan for the river exhibition? I think there are far too many objects in the first room.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I had the same impression. There are almost sixty items in a space that fits perhaps thirty comfortably. People will walk straight past them.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Exactly. But the curator is attached to every single piece. I tried to suggest removing the old fishing nets and she was almost offended.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Maybe we could keep the nets but show them on a screen instead. We could photograph them in high quality and let visitors zoom in.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: That's not a bad idea, although I'm not sure about screens. I find that visitors want to see real things, not just pictures. We've had very good feedback when we let people touch a replica.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That's true. What about making a replica of the net, then? Children could handle it, and the original would be safe behind glass.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: I like that. It would be cheaper than building a whole new display too. Shall we raise it at the meeting on Friday?

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Let's. I'll write a short proposal with some rough costs, and you could add the visitor comments from last year.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Fine. And I'll ask the education team if their volunteers could help to make the replica. They've been looking for a project.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Perfect. If the curator hears that children will enjoy it, I think she'll agree.

parts.title: Part 4 · Talk: Looking after objects
parts.intro: You will hear a museum conservator, Mr Nam, giving a talk to a group of volunteers.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Thank you all for volunteering. Before you begin work in the stores, I'd like to explain the three enemies of every museum object: light, moisture and handling.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Light first. Strong light fades colours and weakens paper and cloth. That's why some of our galleries are so dim. It isn't to create atmosphere, though that's a pleasant side effect. It's to make the objects last for another hundred years.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Second, moisture. If the air is too damp, metal rusts and wood grows mould. If it is too dry, wood cracks and leather becomes hard. So we keep the temperature and the humidity as steady as we can, and steady is more important than perfect.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Third, handling. Believe it or not, clean hands can still cause harm, because skin leaves oils and tiny amounts of acid. For that reason you'll wear gloves for metal and glass, but not for paper, since gloves reduce your feeling and you might tear it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: A rule I'd like you to remember is this: if you aren't sure, don't touch it. Ask me or one of my colleagues. Nobody will think you are foolish. We've all made mistakes, and I once dropped a vase that was two hundred years old. Fortunately I'd put a soft mat beneath it.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Each of you will be given a notebook. If you notice anything unusual, such as a crack, a strange smell, or an insect, write it down and tell me immediately. Small problems found early can be solved.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Now, please follow me to the store, and we'll practise how to carry a tray of objects safely.
